newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN committee takes step towards Iraqi oil deal.
newsitem.headline: UN committee takes step towards Iraqi oil deal.

text.p: The Security Council's sanctions committee on Iraq accepted on Wednesday an oil pricing formula necessary before the new U.N. oil-for-food deal for Iraq can be implemented.
"There were no objections to the pricing formula; therefore it was approved," said U.N. spokesman Ahmad Fawzi.

The United States had blocked adoption of pricing formulas in August and September but U.S. objections were eliminated on Monday after Iraq unconditionally accepted terms of the May 20 accord. The pricing formula dictates the terms of oil sales so that most contracts in the deal can be approved by the experts or overseers without going to the full sanctions committee.
U.S. acceptance removed a key obstacle to allow Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food and aid for civilians suffering from sanctions imposed in 1990.
Approval of the pricing plan for December, however, is not the final step in what has been an arduous process to bring Iraqi oil to world markets for the first time in six years.

Among remaining tasks are inspection of oil metering equipment on Dec. 5 by the Dutch firm Saybolt to ensure faulty equipment at the Zakho station along the Iraq-Turkey border is operational. Lloyds Register personnel were also to inspect facilities this week to ensure its ability to monitor aid imports.

Both companies were expected to report back to the United Nations by mid-December, giving U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali clearance to report the oil deal was ready for implementation before the end of the year.
He reported to the Security Council on Wednesday that most arrangements for the oil-for-food deal were now in place but did not say when the plan would start.

On Monday, Iraq's U.N. ambassador Nizar Hamdoon said he informed the United Nations of "the official Iraqi acceptance" of the terms of the May 20 agreement that outline the deal, called a Memorandum of Understanding.

Iraq had been insisting since mid-October that it control the number, makeup and freedom of movement of U.N. observers who would monitor arrangements on the ground, a stance the U.N. rejected. Baghdad's agreement prompted Washington to drop its policy of blocking the pricing formula adoption.
